Well my name is Robert Clipperton I'm on the steering committee for bus riders of Saskatoon we've got some higher level comments to make regarding city expenditures on city transit first of all who are we well bus riders of Saskatoon was formed 2014 to advocate for better public transit in our city.
We work for transit that's affordable reliable effective and accessible and maintain the transit should be easy.
We're directed by steering committee which meets monthly and supported by a Facebook membership of 845-638 of whom have engaged with the page in the last four months.
This allows us to capture general themes and specific issues of concern to the overall ridership of Saskatoon transit and we're very appreciative that transit management meets with us once a month.
We think of ourselves as a two-way bridge we funnel information on the writer experience to transit management and in turn are able to explain aspects of the transit system to our ridership.
First level of concern is to do with bus replacement we're concerned that sufficient funds may not be spent on bus replacement over the next few years.
We applaud the forward thinking of the previous council when they adopted the fleet replacement strategy.
This was put in place after years of the insufficient investment and a practice of purchasing used buses that were judged to be at their end of their useful lifespan by other jurisdictions.
Neglect of the bus fleet reached a point where the rate of replacement would have required each newly acquired bus to be in service for 87 years.
This lack of attention to the condition of the fleet came to head in 2014 when Saskatoon transit was left with two few roadworthy buses to maintain service on all routes.
A study showed that it's cheaper to buy new buses than to continue the practice of trying to keep old buses running and thus the fleet replacement strategy.

And we fear that the city does not continue with regular investment into new buses we will fall back into the unacceptable service levels which led to the formation of our organization in the first place three years ago.
Second a comment on bus rapid transit were concerned that the majority of the discussion in the press has been about the disruption to BRT at railway crossings.
Some of even maintained that the cost of grade separation at key crossings should be added to the projected cost of any BRT system.

And after discussions with the design consultants were convinced that this is a bit of a red hearing when frequent service was announced for eight straight in 2016 the plan was created with predictions that buses could never run with that degree of frequency.
And that we would see long rates, weights with buses arriving in bunches of two or three and that simply simply hasn't happened.
Those who use the eight straight route myself included are thrilled with the service.
When frequent service was introduced on 22nd straight in July of 2017 they were fewer doom and gloom predictions.
But the problem of railway crossings was pointed to as a fatal flaw and that simply hasn't happened.
We've had virtually no complaints from our members about the effects of the railway crossings on the 22nd straight service.
So it may not be as effective as it would be without a railway crossing but the services still much appreciated.
The bus rapid transit is not about high tech vehicles that are designed to travel at half the speed of light.
It's about ordinary buses that provide a better writer experience due to technological roadway and shelter improvements.
And I think we all need to know that people don't quit using their cars on 22nd straight because there's a chance that a train might block the road for a few minutes on route.
Bus rapid transit can be very effective while we wait for a solution to the railway crossing problem.
And lastly modernizing the system we do wonder if the resource squeeze of the past years and indeed past decades has prevented the system from evolving along with the times.
Reduce service on weekends and evenings is more reflective of the time.
When business says were closed by law and Sundays and evenings and last call in the bars on weekdays was 11 o'clock.

In the morning or later at night than was the case 40 years ago at all of this points to a need to expand service hours on weekends and weekdays some cities have a late night service on Friday and Saturday nights.
Which has the benefit of keeping many drivers who have consumed alcohol off the city streets and we think perhaps the service could be piloted in December of 2018.
